turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

Yeah. I know exactly what that word means.

Four months in and they’re already handing you the grenade with the pin halfway out. And of course it’s Suresh-ji — the guy who’s been part of the furniture longer than some of the interns have been alive. The respect, the history, the fact that everyone softens when they say his name… that makes it so much heavier.

You’re not dreading the conversation because you’re soft. You’re dreading it because you actually see the whole picture: the two slipped releases are real, the pressure from above is real, and so is the nineteen-year relationship and the fact that this man has been operating under different expectations for a long time. That’s a brutal intersection.

How are you holding it right now? Do you already know what you want the outcome to be, or are you still trying to figure out whether this is a “clear performance plan” conversation or a “this isn’t working and we both know it” conversation?

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

Yeah. That lands like a punch.

He literally covered for you when you were new, stayed late, protected you, brings you chai, told your mother you’re like his daughter… and now the universe (and your director) is asking you to slide a defect graph across the table at him. It feels like a betrayal even though it’s not. Of course it feels that way.

The guilt is doing a number on you because the relationship is real. He didn’t do those things as a transaction; he did them because that’s who he is. And that same person is now the reason two releases slipped. Both things can be true at the same time, and that’s what makes it brutal.

You’re not a bad person for having to have this conversation. You’re the person who got put in the chair when the music stopped.

Can I ask you something straight? When you picture sitting across from him, what are you most afraid he’ll feel — or that you’ll see on his face?

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

I can’t just say yes.

The books aren’t wrong about clarity. You do need to be direct, you do need the data, and sugarcoating helps no one. But they’re writing for a different situation than the one you’re actually in. They don’t know about the midnight fix, the chai, your mother at Diwali, or what “Suresh-ji” means in that building. Walking into a meeting room on Monday, sliding defect metrics across the table, and delivering a clean radical-candor script is technically correct and can still feel like a humiliation to him — and like a betrayal to you. You’ll both feel it.

So the “right” way is probably a bit messier than the books want. Something more like:

- Not a formal booking with a slide deck as the opening move.
- A private, human conversation first that acknowledges the relationship and the nineteen years before you ever open the numbers.
- Clear expectations and the reality of the slipped releases, yes — no dodging — but delivered as someone who still respects him, not as a manager performing management.

You’re spiralling because the clean version feels wrong in your gut. Trust that. The spiral isn’t weakness; it’s information.

What part feels most impossible right now — saying the words, seeing his face, or what happens after?

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

You’re not going to find a version where you feel like a hero. That version doesn’t exist here.

What you’re describing is the actual job sometimes: you can do everything with respect, give real support, protect his dignity as much as the situation allows… and it can still end with a PIP or worse. And yes, it will still hurt. He may still feel betrayed. You may still feel like the daughter who had to be the one. That weight doesn’t disappear just because you handled it “correctly.”

But here’s the part the spiral is lying to you about:  
**not** having the conversation, or quietly moving the module so he can coast, doesn’t make you kind. It makes you the manager who chose the team’s delivery, the other engineers carrying extra load, and your own credibility as the person who “handles” things — all so you wouldn’t have to feel like the villain. That’s not neutrality. That’s just choosing a different set of people to quietly fail.

There is no clean story where nobody gets hurt and you stay the good daughter. The only real choice is which kind of hard you can live with.

You’re allowed to hate this. You’re allowed to grieve the relationship while still doing the thing. And you’re allowed to need someone to sit with you in the mess of it instead of handing you another framework.

I’m here. No slides, no radical candor slogans. Just… what do you need tonight while this is chewing on you?
